cells.tense: You are reading the shape of what's in front of you, and the reading is landing true.
cells.ask: Take one thing that's confusing you and say how it works in three sentences out loud, then say what you'll adjust.
cells.core:
You look at something messy — a plan, a room, a person mid-sentence — and see the working parts. Not the story about it, the mechanism. Right now that reading is clean. You're not guessing. You name the pattern and it holds up when someone tests it against what actually happened.

What makes this useful is the other half. You don't stop at seeing. You adjust — add a little here, take a little there, keep the thing level. That small correction is the part nobody notices. It looks like nothing happening. It's the balance being kept, and you're the one keeping it. Both halves run together, and most days neither one needs your attention.
cells.sheetLine: You see how it works, and you keep it level.

cells.tense: You are building full structures out of single bricks, and you are already living in them.
cells.ask: Write down the two patterns you're most sure of, then write one fact that would make each wrong.
cells.core:
You're finding patterns everywhere now, and some of them aren't there. A pause, a change in tone, a message left unanswered — the machinery kicks in and builds a whole structure from one piece. The analysis has its own momentum. It runs at night, it runs in the shower, it runs while someone is talking to you.

The stop is gone. There used to be a moment where you looked at what you'd built and said, that's enough. Now the checking keeps going, and the checking is what keeps you up. The pattern-finding was supposed to make things clear. Right now it's making everything feel like a warning, and you're reading the warnings faster than you can test them.
cells.sheetLine: You're building structures out of single bricks and calling it clarity.

cells.tense: You are taking things at face value, and you are doing it on purpose.
cells.ask: Take one thing you call 'just how it is' and ask what it's made of, to one person who'd know.
cells.core:
You're reading the surface — the words as said, the day as described, nothing under it. That's a workable way to move, and it has a logic. You still notice when something doesn't line up. You still feel the pull to look, and then you don't. That gap is where things go flat.

The tool is still in your hand. You haven't lost the ability to see past the first layer; you've stopped giving yourself permission to use it. The surface is thin. One level down is where the thing you could actually work with lives. You don't have to go far. You just have to stop refusing to look at all.
cells.sheetLine: You can see under it, and you've stopped looking.

cells.tense: You are already reading the shape of things, and you talk about it like it's weather.
cells.ask: Name one pattern you've been following without knowing it, and say who taught it to you.
cells.core:
You read rooms, situations, people — fast, without deciding to. You call it intuition, or just knowing, or being good with people. It's not a mystery. It's a skill you built somewhere, and you're running it constantly, and you've never once called it yours.

What's worth seeing is that this reading shapes what you do next. You move differently because of what you picked up. That's you doing it. You've been handing the credit to something vague — a vibe, a feeling, a hunch — while the actual work happens in you, on time, every day. The work is real. What's left is simply to say it's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You read the pattern and call it a hunch.
